news.title: Donald, Salt turbocharge England's eight-wicket win
news.excerpt: The England openers added 151 off just 61 runs, making short work of the chase against Australia in the 2nd T20I
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Aneurin Donald's blistering 32-ball 85 and Phil Salt's 30-ball 58 powered England to a comprehensive eight-wicket win over Australia in the second T20I at Carrara Oval on Tuesday (November 24). England chased down a target of 185 in just 13.1 overs, registering an emphatic victory and levelling the five-match series at 1-1.

Donald set the tone from the outset, racing to his half-century in just 18 deliveries - the joint third-fastest by an England batter in men's T20Is. Interestingly, the first two overs of the chase brought just 11 runs before Donald went after Jack Edwards, hitting a four and two sixes. Then in the fifth over, he smashed Nikhil Chaudhary for two sixes and two fours to plunder 26. In all, he struck eight fours and six sixes, using his slog sweep to devastating effect.

Salt provided equally destructive support, by taking down Joel Davies for 31 in the eighth over, at the end of which England had 121 on the board and were a canter away from getting home. Salt brought up his own 50 off just 24 balls as the opening pair added 151 in 10 overs.

The partnership had effectively taken the contest away from Australia before either opener was dismissed. Donald eventually fell for 85, while Salt departed for 58, caught and bowled by Ben Dwarshuis. But with only 33 runs required at that stage, there was little left for Australia to contest.

Harry Brook and Tom Banton completed the formalities without any further alarm. Banton struck an unbeaten 20 off just seven deliveries, including two sixes, and finished the chase in style by pulling Nikhil Chaudhary over deep midwicket for six.

Earlier, Australia had recovered from a difficult start to post 184 for 8 after opting to bat. England's bowlers had made early inroads, reducing the hosts to 58 for 4 inside the Powerplay. Adil Rashid was particularly effective through the middle overs, conceding just 26 runs from his four overs and taking the wicket of Lachlan Shaw.

Chaudhary followed up his player of the match winning performance from two nights ago by hitting a 35-ball 45, sharing a 49-run stand with Joel Davies, who contributed 39 off 25 deliveries. Jack Edwards added a quickfire 18 off eight balls, but it was Ben Dwarshuis who gave Australia a late lift, smashing three successive sixes off Sam Curran in the final over to help the hosts finish on 184 for 8.

Curran, despite conceding 20 in his final over, finished with figures of 2 for 29, while Henry Crocombe also claimed two wickets. However, Australia's late surge proved insufficient against an England side that made light work of the chase.

Brief scores: Australia 184/8 in 20 overs (Nikhil Chaudhary 45, Joel Davies 39; Sam Curran 2-29) lost to England 188/2 in 13.1 overs (Aneurin Donald 85, Phil Salt 58; Riley Meredith 1-18) by 8 wickets

news.title: Sinalo Jafta, Marizanne Kapp return for full India series
news.excerpt: South Africa have named eight uncapped players for their one-off Test against India from December 9
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: South Africa will welcome back Sinalo Jafta in all three formats for the home series against India, after she recovered from a hamstring injury that kept her out of the T20I series against Zimbabwe. Experienced all-rounder Marizanne Kapp also makes a comeback to bolster the side. South Africa, under Laura Wolvaardt in all three formats, will host India for a one-off Test, three ODIs and three T20Is in December.

South Africa, who will host their first Test since 2024, have included eight uncapped players to their Test squad: the list includes Alexandra Candler, Oluhle Siyo, Caitlin Wyngaard, all-rounders Eliz-Mari Marx, Nondumiso Shangase and Miané Smit, as well as T20I-capped youngsters Luyanda Nzuza and Nthabiseng Nini.

"It’s a big moment for a player like Alex (Candler), who has earned this opportunity to represent her country at the highest level after doing the business for years at the domestic and Emerging level," South Africa head coach Mandla Mashimbyi said.

"Congratulations also go to Caitlin (Wyngaard), for her selection in the Test and 50-over format. She is a player who has really impressed recently and epitomises the hunger and fight you want to see in a youngster."

"These two players and the other exciting players sprinkled across the three teams, including Yasmeen (Khan) and Oluhle (Siyo) form part of an important bigger picture we have with where we want to take this team. Competition for places is rife, which can only help us along the way,” he concluded.

South Africa Women's Test Squad: Laura Wolvaardt (c), Alexandra Candler, Annerie Dercksen, Marizanne Kapp, Sinalo Jafta, Suné Luus, *Eliz-Mari Marx, Karabo Meso, Nonkululeko Mlaba, Nthabiseng Nini, Luyanda Nzuza, Nondumiso Shangase, Oluhle Siyo, Miané Smit, Caitlin Wyngaard

South Africa Women's ODI Squad: Laura Wolvaardt (c), Anneke Bosch, Tazmin Brits, *Alexandra Candler, Nadine de Klerk, Annerie Dercksen, Marizanne Kapp, Ayabonga Khaka, Sinalo Jafta, Suné Luus, Karabo Meso, Nonkululeko Mlaba, Tumi Sekhukhune, Nondumiso Shangase, Caitlin Wyngaard

South Africa Women's T20I Squad: Laura Wolvaardt (c), Anneke Bosch, Tazmin Brits, Nadine de Klerk, Annerie Dercksen, Sinalo Jafta, Marizanne Kapp, Ayabonga Khaka, Yasmeen Khan, Eliz-Mari Marx, Nonkululeko Mlaba, Seshnie Naidu, Kayla Reyneke, Tumi Sekhukhune, Chloé Tryon, Faye Tunnicliffe

For the white-ball series, South Africa have chosen a settled route by picking a squad largely comprising regulars. In the ODIs, 11 players who featured in the last series - against New Zealand in March-April this year, have been picked. In T20Is too, South Africa have relied on experience in what will be their last series before the inaugural Women's Champions trophy in February 2027.

St. George's Park in Gqeberha will host the one-off Test from December 9 to 12. The two teams will then play three ODIs on December 16, 19 and 22 in Paarl, Cape Town and Bloemfontein respectively. On Boxing Day, the first T20I will be played in Benoni before the action shifts to Potchefstroom where the 2nd and 3rd T20Is will be played on December 29 and 30.

news.title: In a game of big scores, Babar Azam calls for bat-ball balance
news.excerpt: Babar also reckoned that Pakistan are continuing to make good progress despite fledgling results
news.author: Vijay Tagore
body: Babar Azam has enjoyed considerable success in T20 internationals. He is the format's leading run-scorer (4,596) and holds the record for the most 50-plus scores (42). He is also a former ICC No. 1 T20I (in ODIs too) batter. Yet, he advocates for conditions that favour neither the batters nor the bowlers. He seeks balanced conditions.
“They should be friendly for both batters and bowlers – dono ke liye friendly hona chahiye.”

His observations come at a juncture when the game appears increasingly tilted in favour of batters – smaller boundaries, better bats and fielding restrictions. It is a time when 60 in the first six overs is considered a decent start and a 75-run Powerplay is brilliant.

In New Zealand recently, India scored 178 for 2 in 10 overs in a T20I game after reaching 118 for no loss in the Powerplay. In the IPL earlier this year, there were multiple 250-plus totals and on one occasion, a 260-plus target was chased.

“It all depends on the conditions. It is right in front of you. Where are you playing? What conditions are you playing in? Every country and every venue has a different scoring pattern. In some places, the par score is 200 or more, while in others, it is different,” Babar, who has opened in 87 of his 136 T20I innings, tells Cricbuzz.

“So, you should play according to the conditions. What we have learnt about those conditions and what we talk about matters. Where the conditions demand 200, we will look to score 200-plus. Where there is no need to score 200-plus, you can even get 100 and be competitive.”

Babar’s other credentials in T20Is are as impeccable. Pakistan’s most-capped T20I player (145), he is also the third most experienced T20I captain in the world, having led his country in 85 matches. He also holds the record for captaining Pakistan in 55 consecutive T20Is. He has a record of nine consecutive 50-plus scores across formats - a world record (March 2022 - June 2022).

Babar is currently featuring in the ILT20 for the first time in its five-season history and made an immediate impact, smashing 86 in his debut game to earn the Player of the Match award as his side coasted to a comfortable win over Sharjah Warriorz.

The Vipers franchise is based in Dubai, in the UAE, a country that played a significant role in Babar's early international career. It was here that he made his Test debut in October 2016, after scoring three consecutive centuries in September and October that year in Sharjah and Abu Dhabi. The UAE also holds special memories for him as the venue where he led Pakistan to a memorable 10-wicket victory over India in a T20 World Cup encounter in 2021.

“I have fond memories of the place. They are very good memories. The best memories are, of course, those three consecutive centuries. They changed my career. For me, those are the best moments of my cricketing journey. The World Cup win against India in Dubai was memorable too. Pakistan won by 10 wickets, chasing 152 without losing a wicket, with Mohammad Rizwan and me opening the batting.”

Since that game in 2021, Pakistan managed to beat India only once in nine T20Is and never in three ODIs. Has Pakistan cricket genuinely progressed in the last five years? They have managed to beat India only once in nine meetings since in T20Is and trail 0-3 in ODIs.

But Babar believes progress has been made. “It is all in front of you. Progress is needed everywhere, and we are working towards it. You must have seen our recent Test wins.” Pakistan recently beat Sri Lanka in a two-Test series at home.

He is, however, reluctant to look too far ahead, whether to next year's World Cup in South Africa or to Pakistan's prospects of qualifying for the World Test Championship final in the next cycle. For now, he insists, his focus is entirely on the ILT20.

Babar is one of Pakistan's most closely followed cricketers and is also subject to considerable scrutiny. He prefers not to dwell on that, choosing instead to acknowledge the support he receives from fans. “I'm very lucky. Alhamdulillah, people have supported me, and I try to maintain that support through my performances.”

news.title: Mitchell, Ronchi pleased with NZ's ability to dig into their reserve at the Basin
news.excerpt: Daryl Mitchell played out 258 balls with Glenn Phillips in a sixth-wicket partnership to force a draw
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: New Zealand's escape in Wellington was put down by Daryl Mitchell to staying in the moment and repeating the same thing, ball after ball, for as long as it took. The hosts trailed by 352 after India made the highest Test total ever scored against New Zealand, and once a result was out of reach, their only job was to bat out time.

They did it over 120 overs and 557 minutes, with Mitchell and Glenn Phillips seeing off 43 overs together on the final day. New Zealand haven't had to do that often. The last time they batted and battled through to a draw was in Kanpur in 2021, when Rachin Ravindra and Ajaz Patel held on for the last wicket.

"I think just trying to be as present as you can," Mitchell said a day after the draw, "And watch the ball and try and repeat that for long periods of time. I guess the nature of this side is we play a lot of cricket with each other, so we know what makes each other tick as well. So, I mean, it's just being present, repeating it ball after ball after ball. It might be boring at times, but yeah, nice to get the job done.
"I love batting with a GP, across all three formats, it's seriously good fun and it was nice to do, I guess, a different style for both of us."

Neither Mitchell nor Phillips is a natural blocker, and it was their restraint that pleased batting coach Luke Ronchi most. "It's adaptability," he said. "You know your role and what you want to do in each moment. I think the way Rachin Ravindra goes about it, the way Daryl Mitchell goes about it, the way GP goes about it, it's all very different. But you also know that in those moments they're doing whatever's needed for the team and that's a pretty cool thing as well.

"The guys know how to bat long periods of time. It's making sure there's different things that were going through their minds. We chat to both of them [Mitchell and Phillips], there are times where they want to give it a whack and do something, have a bit of an ego about it, but to be able to pull that back and know that this is what's needed in the moment, I think it's fantastic.

"We haven't really been in a position like that before, especially in the time I've been involved. So I think, it's sort of, to take it forward into the next Test now and that in different situations we can adapt and make the most of those opportunities."
New Zealand also had help from the Basin Reserve surface, which got flatter and easier to bat on as the match went on. However, Mitchell expects the Hagley Oval in Christchurch to be livelier.

"The nature of the Basin surface is it usually starts pretty green," Mitchell said. "We probably didn't expect it to get that slow and low over the course of five days, but now we're here at Hagley and I'm sure there might be a bit of bounce in this one."

India took only three of the eight wickets they needed on the final day and shook hands shortly after the last hour began. Ronchi said the timing surprised him a little, but he understood the reasoning.

"Their bowlers had all bowled 50 overs [each in the match]. It's looking at the bigger picture of things and their fast bowlers have put in a lot of work. So each side has their ways of thinking about how you might try and get the result. So for them to do it the way they did, they felt that was the right way."

news.title: Priyansh Arya shatters records in 181-run blitz against TN
news.excerpt: The Delhi opener struck 19 sixes, equalling Finn Allen’s record for the most in a single T20 innings
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Priyansh Arya rewrote the record books with a scintillating 181 that blew Tamil Nadu away at the Daly College Ground in Indore. Priyansh’s 68-ball knock was studded with 19 sixes - the joint-highest for a player in an individual T20 innings - as he finished with the second-highest individual T20 score behind Lhuan-dre Pretorius’ 188*. The Delhi skipper powered his team to a massive 275/5 before Tamil Nadu were bowled out for 159 - 22 fewer than Priyansh’s own score.

Karan Lal’s unbeaten 29-ball 82 powered Bengal to a crushing win over Uttar Pradesh in Mumbai. In a game reduced to 15 overs per side, Lal and Abishek Porel (69 off 39) led a stunning onslaught as Bengal posted 201, with Bhuvneshwar Kumar, Kuldeep Yadav and Divyansh Joshi going for plenty. UP never got going in the chase and were restricted to 108/7.

Mohammed Azharuddeen and Rohan Kunnummal struck rapid fifties as Kerala cruised to a nine-wicket win over Assam in Mohali. Offspinner Vaisakh Chandran did the star turn with 3 for 20 with the ball as Assam were limited to 165/5. Azharuddeen then smashed an unbeaten 93 off 37, his partnership with Kunnummal worth 123 in just 8.1 overs.

Goa posted a solid 196/6, but Chhattisgarh managed to seal a tight four-wicket win in the final over thanks to Amandeep Khare’s 116. While fifties from Abhinav Tejrana and Lalit Yadav headlined Goa’s batting effort, Khare singlehandedly led Chhattisgarh’s response, before Dev Aditya Singh and Vijay Yadav struck crucial cameos to seal the chase.
More to follow...

news.title: Babar Azam's 86 steers Desert Vipers to first win
news.excerpt: Paul Walter’s 75 went in vain as Sharjah Warriorz succumbed to their second consecutive defeat
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Babar Azam unleashed his best with a chanceless 51-ball 86 on ILT20 debut as Desert Vipers completed a comfortable six-wicket win over Sharjah Warriorz in Sharjah on Monday (November 23). The win fetched the defending champions their first points, while consigning the Warriorz to their second consecutive loss early in the season.

The Vipers restricted the Warriorz to 166, before Babar got the chase going with a couple of boundaries off Adam Milne in the opening over. It was followed by two more fours in the second over and another in the third as he cashed in on anything remotely loose. A 39-run opening stand with Fakhar Zaman was brought to a halt by Junaid Siddique as the southpaw perished for 15. But Babar and Andries Gous put Milne under the pump in a 22-run over, before the former wrapped up a 70-run Powerplay with a six.

Gous fell immediately after but the start that the Vipers got off to allowed them to consolidate through the middle-overs. Babar raised a 31-ball fifty and continued to bat with purpose, slogsweeping Sikandar Raza for a six before reeling off a couple of fours off Siddique. Soon came three boundaries in the space of four balls against Ali Naseer as the Vipers raced past 150 in the 15th over. Joe Clarke, who gave Babar company in an 82-run stand, fell to Milne, who also brought the Babar masterclass to an end in the same over. But the outcome was an inevitable one as the Vipers crossed the finish line with 15 balls to spare.

Earlier, the Warriorz raced away in the Powerplay after being asked to bat first as Walter and Tim Seifert tore into Mujeeb Ur Rahman in a 19-run second over. Babar made his presence felt very early, completing a diving catch to remove Seifert. But it did not stop Walter from continuing to make an impression as an opener, hammering a 101-metre six off Naseem Shah too as the Powerplay produced 77 runs. The spinners applied the brakes as no boundary followed for the next three overs, before Walter smashed Mujeeb for a six to get to his fifty.

The Warriorz were still well placed at 96/1 at the halfway mark, but completely lost their way thereafter. James Vince fell for a scratchy 23, before Shadab Khan bagged two more, removing Brandon McMullen and Sikandar Raza in the same over to finish with 3/18. Once Walter was bowled by a Naseem yorker for a 43-ball 75, the wheels came off as wickets fell at regular intervals. Khuzaima Tanveer bagged three of his own, and the innings fittingly culminated in a run out as the Warriorz lost their last eight wickets for 44 runs.

Brief Scores: Sharjah Warriorz 166 in 20 overs (Paul Walter 75; Shadab Khan 3-18, Khuzaima Tanveer 3-31, Tom Curran 2-25) lost to Desert Vipers 167/4 in 17.3 overs (Babar Azam 86, Joe Clarke 35; Adam Milne 2-42, Waqar Salamkheil 1-26) by 6 wickets.

news.title: Farcical finish caps Basin's rare benign offering
news.excerpt: India would have fancied taking the series lead after the first session. But on a lifeless deck, even that proved wishful thinking after all
news.author: Bharat Sundaresan
body: It was a farcical finish befitting of what had been a farcical surface for a Test match. Dhruv Jurel bowling long-hops and getting cheered by a clearly bored slip cordon. Jasprit Bumrah ambling back to the field after having been off it for nearly eight overs. The rest of the Indian team floating around the Basin Reserve outfield that had witnessed a glut of runs over the previous five days. And Shubman Gill had started stripping off the tape that he wears around his fingers even before Jurel had bowled the final delivery to Glenn Phillips.

The umpires were just about to call for drinks to signal for the final hour or the start of the mandatory overs, only for Gill to signal to Daryl Mitchell that his team was done. They’d had enough of toiling away on a thankless pitch that had refused to deteriorate, forget crumble. At least in the way they needed it to for the eight wickets they’d required at the start of the day.

There’s been some criticism of Gill’s decision to pull the plug with 90 legal deliveries still left in the Test. But that’s disregarding the extent to how benign this deck was. So much so that a couple of the New Zealand bowlers would listen to every pitch report that took place in the mornings and quiz the broadcasters as to what plans they might have for success on this bizarrely uncharacteristic Basin surface. “Here for any idea, because I have none,” one of them said pretty plainly.

There were a few signs leading up to Gill’s decision to call it off that the visitors had grudgingly acknowledged the inevitability of their mission on Monday. After having thrown the ball around to his fast bowlers in the final session, which started with the Black Caps needing to survive 39 overs, Gill finally brought Akash Deep back on after a couple of brief bursts from Bumrah and Prasidh Krishna.

But this was to be a one-over spell for Deep, as Mitchell in particular looked alarmingly at ease against the seam bowler. Like he had against every Indian bowler, including Bumrah with the fresh second new-ball and also later in the final session as the genius fast bowler tried honing into his stumps. By the next over, Gill had left the field as well to join Bumrah, as KL Rahul took over the reins for the next few overs as the ball started getting thrown around to the part-timers, the real part-timers too in Yashasvi Jaiswal followed by Jurel.

This was also the phase when Washington Sundar was allowed to get his way for a DRS on an lbw shout where one of the close-in fielders guessed beforehand that the review would show “all three greens” and Rishabh Pant had shouted, “that’s pitching outside leg-stump, mate” in his best Aussie accent. How right they were. The ball had pitched way outside leg-stump.

The wheels were coming off, and you couldn’t blame the Indians who had tried everything they could, a few times over as well, but to no avail. Maybe it was the new ground-staff or the fact that windy Wellington didn’t live up to its moniker for the first four days, the moisture content not being consistent with what’s generally the case here, or the wrong colour of grass-cover at the start. There was no dearth of theories in the end but the fact was that the Basin had not produced a surface this flat and dull in a long time. Even the cracks that began to develop understandably towards the end of Day 4 were intact enough for the plates not to move or for even the edges of the cracks to disintegrate enough for the ball to misbehave to any extent.

The only times the Indian bowlers felt like they could be in the game was when a few deliveries from the RA Vance Stand skid through and kept low, one of them getting the better of Tom Blundell. But even that aspect of the challenge was negated when the second new ball was taken, with the hardness of the ball allowing Mitchell and Phillips to trust their defence and the consistency of the bounce off the pitch.

There was the one chance that went down late in the second session as a delivery from Kamboj caught Mitchell on the gloves after jumping at him off a length but evaded Devdutt Padikkal’s extended hand at short leg. One of maybe five times the Indians would get excited on a tiring final day where the draw began to emerge as the most likely result from around halfway through the second session.

India had done a lot right in the first session to get rid of the overnight batters, Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra, and at that point they would have fancied themselves to go on to take a 1-0 lead. In hindsight, that was probably wishful thinking on a surface where 407 overs were bowled and only 24 wickets fell across five days, five of which came within the first 29 overs of the match.

news.title: Tickner ruled out of second India Test with hamstring injury
news.excerpt: Matt Fisher has been named his replacement for the Christchurch Test beginning on November 27
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Blair Tickner has been ruled out of the second Test against India after suffering a right hamstring injury during a training session in Wellington this week.
The New Zealand fast bowler will undergo further assessments in Christchurch on Monday to determine the extent of the injury and establish an expected return-to-play timeline.

Matt Fisher has been named as Tickner's replacement in the squad. Fisher, who featured in New Zealand's T20I and ODI series against India, will join the team in Christchurch ahead of the second Test, which begins on Friday at the Hagley Oval.
The first Test match in Wellington ended in a draw.

news.title: A green nightmare for Bangladesh as South Africa run riot
news.excerpt: Anrich Nortjé marked his return with a fiery spell as Bangladesh were bundled out for 91 on a testing Centurion surface
news.author: Telford Vice
body: Sage? Olive? Fern? Mint? Pistachio? There are, one source says, 134 different shades of green. Another lists 20 “core definitions” of the colour and 23 “non-biological” versions. Among the latter are “India” and “Islamic” green.

What would Centurion’s pitch for the second Test between South Africa and Bangladesh be called? “Jungle”? “Army”? “Swamp”? “Screamin’”? Certainly not “fun”. For batters, at any rate. More like “deathly”. Those are all in the glossary of green names.

The latter was coined after arsenic-based green paint killed many in the 18th and 19th centuries. Napoleon Bonaparte’s cause of death has been listed as stomach cancer. But unnaturally high levels of arsenic — which has been linked to an increased risk of gastric carcinoma — were found in his hair after his death on May 5, 1821. The walls of the house in St Helena in which he died were painted his favourite colour: bright green.
Whatever the name of the shade of the Centurion pitch — someone suggested it was a combination of maybe 120 of the 134 — it was the certainly, undeniably, utterly green.

So there was only one thing for it when Aiden Markram, standing in for the injured Temba Bavuma, called correctly. That marked the first time in five Tests this season that South Africa have won the toss. We’ll field, thank you, Markram told Andy Pycroft. Not least because that meant not having to bat first.

“Even at 53 and at 115 [kilometres an hour] I’d fancy bowling on that surface,” Shaun Pollock said on the broadcast before the start of play, which rain delayed by three hours and 40 minutes. Thing is, Pollock’s comment also boomed on the ground’s sound system. It wasn’t what Tanzid Hasan and Mahfijul Islam would have wanted to hear as they checked their pad straps and thumping hearts and prepared to open the batting.

Anticipation grew in the lush air as Kagiso Rabada stood at the top of his mark and waited for Tanzid to take guard. The crowd that waited with him was small but buzzing and chuffed with themselves for waiting out the weather. Now they wanted a reward.
Rabada swooped swanlike and bowled … the ball pitched well short and well wide of Tanzid, and was duly damned as a wide by Ahsan Raza.
South Africa made their advantage count 11 deliveries later. Marco Jansen produced an inswinger that induced an indecisive drive from Tanzid. The edge flew to first slip.
By tea the visitors had crumbled, like a stale scone, to 85/6. They were put out of their misery 39 balls into the third session, having added a piddling six more runs.
Rabada, though threatening in his opening burst of six overs, went wicketless for 22. Then he took 3/1 across 17 deliveries.

But South Africa’s fast bowling kudos belong to Anrich Nortjé, who hadn’t played since limping off with a groin injury during the second Test against Australia at St George’s Park last month. He set the tone by nailing Mahfijul Islam’s off-stump with an inswinger timed at 143 kilometres-an-hour. Two balls later Nortjé delivered the same dose to Najmul Hossain Shanto, this time with a straightening delivery that streaked past the Bangladesh captain at 142 km/h.
Nortjé and injuries are depressingly well acquainted. Given his assorted calamities, how was he able to trust his body to be able to let fly in the manner to which we have all become accustomed?

“You just feel things are good again and you’ve just got to back it,” Nortjé told a press conference. “You can’t hold back and worry about X, Y and Z. So You’ve just got to back it, go with how you’re feeling, give the feedback to [the medical staff] you’re working with, and then try and progress as quickly as possible and make the best of it. At the end of the day you've just got to back it.”

But back to the pitch. To be fair to it and its creator, Brian Bloy, there was nothing unfair about the surface. There was plenty of bounce but no undue movement. There was a touch of swing but that invariably is the case when Centurion’s skies are clouded.

The issue is that Bangladesh don’t often play in conditions like these. On their only other visit to this ground, in November 2008, they made 250 and 131 and were beaten by an innings inside three days. Unsurprisingly nobody from that XI is in the current team. Even if they were, how much might they remember from a single match played 18 years ago?
That said, Bangladesh scored 400 in the first innings at the Wanderers last week. How did that square with being shot out for 91 in 33.3 overs on Monday?

“There were some good balls out there but not enough for us to be rolled over like that,” Malibongwe Maketa told a press conference. “We worked really hard, especially coming here without much preparation. The way the guys showed guts and determination [in Johannesburg] was really pleasing, and we wanted to build on that.
“Unfortunately today was not the day. We know the guys have got it technically. We can make better decisions on wickets like that.

“Doing well at the Wanderers, and then coming here and losing the toss after a long rain delay, mentally you have to be up for it. We were really behind the eight-ball mentally, which was disappointing.”

Maketa isn’t the only South African in Bangladesh’s dressing room. Dale Benkenstein is also there. Surely they would have prepared their charges for the challenges of batting in Centurion. Had the message landed, or had their players not listened?

“I think the message has landed,” Maketa said. “You can talk as much as you can but it boils down to performance. Players have to go over the rope and apply themselves. It’s up to us to take the responsibility for that as coaches. We have to get better.”
Was Nortjé surprised that a team who had batted solidly down the road a few days ago could look all at sea?

“No; conditions were very different at the Wanderers,” Nortjé said. “And as much as we can wonder how they’re going to perform, it’s still Test cricket. Every team can perform well. You’ve just got to control the controllables. Maybe from the outside you can overthink it, but from the inside it’s just to try and keep it as simple as possible.”

The sun shouldered the clouds aside while Monday’s car crash was lurching through its episodes. Brightness was all around by the time Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman walked out to bat, making the Bangladeshis’ job still harder.

Markram drove the second ball of the innings through the covers for four with the kind of authority that said he wanted to fix what had gone wrong in his last 15 innings, only two of which yielded 50. Neither of them grew to a century.

He hit four more boundaries — through mid-off, square leg, midwicket and mid-off again — before trying to pull a wide one from Ebadot Hossain and steering it, via the toe of his bat, to Litton Das. All but one of his 21 had come in fours.

Markram had seemed cleared for take-off, with all but a single of his 21 off 23 flowing in fours. Hence it took him an age to leave the scene. Maybe he was counting, as he trudged, the 80-odd runs he had left out there.

What might Markram have made of Ackerman, who in his first five innings as an opener — he never batted there in his 134 trips to the first-class crease before making his Test debut against Australia at St George’s Park — scored six, 95, 62, 157 and nought. When bad light ended play on Monday he was four runs short of another half-century.

Markram would do well not to think about the fact that Ackerman should have been out for one, when the visitors didn’t refer a leg-before appeal that would have been successful, and two, when Towhid Hridoy dropped a dipping but catchable chance at first slip.

Reality, not imaginings, is what matters now. And the reality is South Africa are three runs behind with nine wickets in hand. That’s enough to turn any opponents any shade of green you could think of.

news.title: Maketa rues Bangladesh's poor decision-making after 91 all out
news.excerpt: The Bangladesh assistant coach believes poor decision-making and a lack of mental preparation contributed to their collapse on the opening day.
news.author: Atif Azam
body: Bangladesh assistant coach Malibonge Maketa said that they are disappointed to be bowled out for less than 100 runs in their first innings against South Africa in the second Test as he feels decision making played a big part in it.
South Africa took firm control of the second Test as they raced to 88 for 1 in 17 overs after bowling Bangladesh out for just 91 in 33.3 overs on a rain-hit opening day in Centurion.

“Yeah, it was a very disappointing day overall. I mean, the scorecard tells that. For us, it's more or less the decision-making which equates to some soft dismissals. There were some good balls out there, but not enough for us to be rolled over like that,” said Maketa.

“We've worked really hard, especially coming here in the first Test with not much preparation. The way the guys showed guts and determination was really pleasing and we wanted to build on that. Unfortunately, today was not the day and yeah, we'll have to sit back and see where we can improve, especially decision-making because we know technically guys have got it. We can maybe make better decisions on wickets like that,” he said.
Maketa added that they lacked the mentality that was required to battle it out on a green wicket.
“Losing the toss after a long rain delay, mentally you have to be up for it with the short turnaround time when you have to go out and bat,” said Maketa.
“Today probably one of the days where we were not, we were really behind the eight ball in terms of that mentally, which was quite disappointing,” he said.

“We've been really working hard in terms of patterns of dismissals. I mean, South Africa is also watching. They know where they want to bowl, we know where they're going to bowl and we've really been working hard in terms of eliminating those mistakes,” he said.

“If you look at the dismissals, they are mental mistakes as Ken I think pointed it out earlier, they are mental mistakes. And for us, we know if we go through our processes and we actually give ourselves the best opportunity to perform and leave early on in our innings, we're going to be more successful, but we haven't really got that game plan nailed down yet on the bouncy wickets, which has been disappointing,” he added.
Maketa added that the top-order must take responsibility to allow Litton Das to bat with more freedom while adding that he will have a chat with Towhid Hridoy regarding his dismissal.

Litton, after surviving a reprieve, chased another wide delivery from Marco Jansen in the next over and edged it to gully while Hridoy briefly counter-attacked Harmer but threw his wicket away on the final delivery before Tea, charging down the track and edging the ball to slip.

“Litton has really done well for us, especially in this cycle. He's a really good player. Obviously, we can't expect runs to come from the same person all the time. He will make mental mistakes, today was one of those days. He's one of our best players. We really need to just make sure that we get into games. Him coming in with four down all the time, it's not going to help his cricket, it's not going to help our game plan. We really need to take responsibility from other batters to make sure that they do their job for Litton to be able to do his job,” said Maketa.

“Currently, he's finding himself batting under pressure every time, which is not ideal, especially in conditions like this. That's where each and every one of the batters have to take more responsibility in terms of their roles and responsibility and it hasn't happened as much as we would like,” he said.

“I still haven't had a chat with him (Hridoy) yet. I don't know what he was thinking. When I get back in the changing room, we usually leave each other alone when he's played something like that, which he did against the West Indies first test. I gave him a bit of time. I'm sure tonight he'll be the one coming to me and talking. So after I've chatted to him, we can have that conversation,” he said.

“We are still working with a lot of the players in terms of just getting through that mental routine of breathing when they're starting their innings and making sure they're getting through their processes before the ball is bowled. If you look at how we are rushed between overs and how we are rushed between balls, those are the small things that play a big part in how a batter structures his innings. So we're pointing it out, we're working on them and I'm sure we will get it right,” he said.

news.title: Ruthless South Africa dominate opening day in Centurion
news.excerpt: Despite losing the first session to rain, South Africa went into stumps trailing by just 3 runs
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: South Africa produced a dominant display against Bangladesh on the first day of the second Test at Centurion. After the entirety of the first session was lost due to intermittent showers, South Africa bowled Bangladesh out for just 91 before nearly wiping out the deficit by Stumps. Bangladesh’s innings lasted just 33.3 overs, with each of the five South African bowlers picking up at least one wicket.

South Africa won the toss and unsurprisingly opted to bowl under overcast skies after the start of play was delayed by more than three hours due to rain. Marco Jansen struck first, drawing an outside edge from Tanzid Hasan Tamim in the second over. Mahfijul Islam struck consecutive boundaries off Kagiso Rabada to begin the third over but never really looked settled with the ball beating the bat on several occasions. He struck a couple more streaky boundaries before being knocked over by Anrich Nortje in the 14th over.

Back in the side after another injury layoff, Nortje removed Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto just two balls later. Wickets kept tumbling thereafter with Wiaan Mulder getting Mominul Haque to chop on in the 21st over. Jansen returned to claim his second by having Litton Das out caught behind in the 26th before Simon Harmer, who had been struck for a six, had Towhid Hridoy caught at slip in the next and final over of the session.

Down 85 for 6 at Tea, Bangladesh’s resistance was short-lived with Kagiso Rabada ripping through the lower order. He dismissed Shoriful Islam, Jaker Ali and Taskin Ahmed in his first, second and third overs of the session respectively before Jansen wrapped the innings up by scalping Khaled Ahmed.

South Africa got off to a brisk start with the openers striking a flurry of boundaries inside the first seven overs. Aiden Markram, who had survived an appeal for LBW on review in the second over and had gotten off to a solid start since, was the first and only South African batter to fall as he was out edging behind to Ebadot Hossain in the ninth over.

Having already offered Marques Ackerman a reprieve in the third over by virtue of not referring an appeal for LBW that would’ve been out, Bangladesh also dropped Zubayr Hamza in the 11th. The Bangladeshi bowlers also struggled for control, conceding 12 extras, 11 of which were wides. Ackerman batted with great freedom and remained unbeaten on 46 off just 53 deliveries as South Africa ended the day on 88 for 1, just three runs behind Bangladesh.
Brief Scores: Bangladesh 91 all-out (Mahfijul Islam 23; Marco Jansen 3-17, Kagiso Rabada 3-23) lead South Africa 88/1 (Marques Ackerman 46*, Aiden Markram 21; Ebadot Hossain 1-19) by 3 runs.

news.title: Peshawar to make PSL debut by hosting 2027 season opener
news.excerpt: The city was originally scheduled to host games last season but will make its long-awaited bow in the coming year
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Peshawar is set to host Pakistan Super League matches for the first time since the tournament’s inception. Confirmed as one of the six venues for the upcoming edition, it will also stage the opening fixture. The city has not hosted an international fixture since 2006.  The early seasons of the PSL were largely held in the UAE with matches held in Dubai, Sharjah and Abu Dhabi. Lahore, Karachi, Rawalpindi and Multan have hosted matches in subsequent editions.  A six-city schedule, which included Faisalabad and Peshawar, had been planned for last season but was shelved amid the conflict in West Asia and the ensuing fuel crisis. The 2026 edition was subsequently split between Lahore and Karachi, with all matches played behind closed doors.  “This is a moment the league, and above all the fans of Peshawar, have been looking forward to for twelve years. Peshawar's love for cricket is unmatched, and PSL 12 will finally give that passion the stage it deserves. Adding a sixth venue is a major step in the growth of the league, and we look forward to delivering a memorable experience for every fan who walks into the stadium,” said PSL CEO Salman Naseer.  “Peshawar has waited a long time for this and its fans have waited with patience and passion. Bringing the PSL to Peshawar is about recognising what this city has given to Pakistan cricket and giving its people the chance to celebrate the game at home. I am confident the people of Peshawar will welcome the league with the energy and warmth they are known for,” said PCB Chairman Mohsin Naqvi. The full schedule for the upcoming edition is yet to be announced.

news.title: Nahid Rana misses South Africa ODIs despite medical clearance
news.excerpt: Litton Kumar Das returns to the squad as he is all set to begin his tenure as full-time ODI captain
news.author: Atif Azam
body: The Bangladesh team management has opted to take a cautious approach with Nahid Rana, leaving the fast bowler out of the ODI squad for the upcoming three-match series against South Africa despite him receiving clearance from the Australian medical team.

Bangladesh ODI captain Litton Kumar Das returns to the squad and the series will mark the beginning of his tenure as full-time captain, having yet to lead the side in the 50-over format since being appointed to the role.
Along with Litton, batters Naim Sheikh, Yasir Ali Chowdhury and Jaker Ali Anik, as well as pacer Syed Khaled Ahmed, have also returned to the squad.

Rana was expected to return for the ODI series after recently arriving home following a lengthy rehabilitation stint in Australia. However, the team management has preferred not to rush him back. "We don't want to push him. We know he is one of our premier bowlers and we have to understand how we want to get the most out of him. So we felt there is no need to hurry, as he is just returning from an injury and we want him to get sufficient time to get ready," a member of the selection panel said.

Cricbuzz understands that the national team management will soon decide on Rana's participation in the three-match T20I series against South Africa. A section of the think tank feel there is little point in rushing him back for the shorter format and would rather take the necessary steps to ensure he is fully fit ahead of the two-match Test series against England, scheduled for February.

Saif Hassan, Soumya Sarkar, Musaddek Hossain Saikat, Nurul Hasan Sohan and off-spinner Aliss Al Islam, who earned his maiden ODI call-up for the UAE series, have failed to retain their places. Hasan Mahmud has also been left out after sustaining an elbow injury during the opening Test against South Africa earlier this week.
Parvez Hossain Emon, meanwhile, retains his place in the squad.

Squad - Litton Kumer Das (Captain), Tanzid Hasan, Parvez Hossain Emon, Naim Sheikh, Najmul Hossain Shanto, Tawhid Hridoy (Vice Captain), Yasir Ali Chowdhury, Jaker Ali Anik, Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Tanvir Islam, Rishad Hossain, Syed Khaled Ahmed, Taskin Ahmed, Mustafizur Rahman, Shoriful Islam.
