news.title: 'It started in Durban, not in PE' - de Villiers pushes back Australia's tampering timeline
news.excerpt: De Villiers was at the crease when the incident was caught on camera in the second Test
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: AB de Villiers believes Australia's tampering of the ball during the 2018 series in South Africa started a Test earlier than recent accounts suggest - in the series opener at Durban rather than in Port Elizabeth.

The episode has been back in the news for a little over a fortnight, after Usman Khawaja's autobiography Sabr brought it up again. Since then, Khawaja, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft have each described in detail how sandpaper was used on the ball in the second Test at what is now Gqeberha, a match before Bancroft was caught on camera at Newlands.

De Villiers was closer to the action than most. He made a hundred against the reversing ball in Port Elizabeth, and he was at the crease in Cape Town when Bancroft was found with the sandpaper. He now says the problem goes back to the opening Test of the series.

"It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE," de Villiers said on his podcast. "And I'm very happy for people to quote me on that. We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead.

"Trust me, I've played a lot of cricket there. So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or a nail or I don't care. I honestly do not care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew.
"The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn't just reverse. It's not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, 'guys, we were wrong'."

That doesn't match Bancroft's account. In a long first-person piece published last week, the opener said Australia did not use sandpaper in Durban, a Test in which Mitchell Starc's reverse swing did much of the damage. He did, however, admit that other methods were in play.

"Casting forward to the first Test in Durban, sandpaper was not used," he wrote. "There were more traditional methods of maintaining the ball, including saliva. I cannot say with certainty whether mints or lollies were involved. Probably quarter-seam picking, this practice became so normal after my first Test.

"Importantly for the chronology of events, I was not responsible for the ball in that Test. However, what happened in the second Test in Port Elizabeth was different. It was a significant escalation. And it was where I became directly involved."

Australia had noticed how early the ball started moving at the time. Speaking after the opening day, when the visitors batted first, David Warner said, "We didn't assess for reverse [swing] in the first day - not after 24 or 25 overs."

For de Villiers, the recent focus on which tool was used misses the point entirely. "It's the weirdest thing because everyone's talking about the sandpaper now," he said. "That's the point everyone's missing at the moment. And it confuses me so much. Why are we all so worried about the object that was used? The fact of the matter is there was a premeditated decision made to do something illegal on the ground. And every single person knew about it. I've zero per cent doubt about it."
He was quick to admit that South Africa, and he himself, also looked for every advantage with the old ball. But he drew a firm line at what Australia did.

"I'm not playing all innocent and saying that I'm the perfect person," he said. "We all try and get the ball to reverse. We try and bounce it in. We try and do it in a legal manner and we try and push the boundaries as much as possible.

"So I'm not this beautiful angel trying to say that he's wrong and he's wrong and he's wrong. We all have tried over the years to get the ball to do something, to get an edge, but obviously not being as stupid as to take an object onto the field and blatantly cheating."

news.title: WTC Scenarios: India's hopes dented after Wellington draw
news.excerpt: Even a clean sweep of their remaining six Tests will leave Gill's side seeking favours from other teams
news.author: Roshan Gede
body: The high-scoring stalemate between New Zealand and India in Wellington has resulted in a dip in points percentage for both teams in the ICC World Test Championship standings, with New Zealand slipping from second to third. It is India's chances, however, that have taken a significant hit, with just six games remaining for the two-time runners-up.

West Indies, Sri Lanka and Pakistan are no longer in contention for a top-two finish. Here are the updated WTC scenarios for the other six teams following the Wellington result. All scenarios below assume no further points deductions for slow over rates.
South Africa
Remaining fixtures: BAN (1 Test, home), ENG (3 Tests, home), SL (2 Tests, away)

South Africa remain top of the table with six wins from eight games, and can consolidate their position further should they beat Bangladesh in the second Test in Centurion, starting Monday. Five wins out of six, or four wins and two draws, will guarantee them a top-two finish. Even three wins out of six would leave them in a reasonable position, with a points percentage of between 64.29 and 71.43, depending on how many of the other three Tests they lose or manage to draw. Their next major series is against England, whom they haven't beaten in a home Test series this century – they lost in 2004/05, 2015/16 and 2019/20, and drew in 2009/10.
However, their current form makes them favourites to change that and seal a spot in a second straight final.
Australia
Remaining fixtures: NZ (4 Tests, home), IND (5 Tests, away)

Australia can reach a maximum points percentage of 81.82 if they win all nine, and even seven wins would seal them a place in the final (unless both defeats come against New Zealand and the Blackcaps win all their other games). While they have had a dominant record against New Zealand for over a decade – nine wins and a draw in 10 Tests since 2015 – they have struggled in India. Since their series victory there in 2004/05, Australia have won two, lost 12 and drawn four Tests in India.
Five wins and four defeats would see them finish on 63.64. That is still a decent position, but it would leave them dependent on several other results.
New Zealand
Remaining fixtures: IND (1 Test, home), AUS (4 Tests, away), SL (2 Tests, home), PAK (2 Tests, away)
Six wins and three draws, or a minimum of seven wins, will guarantee the Blackcaps a place in the final.

A stiff challenge awaits in Australia after the India series, and their recent head-to-head record, as mentioned previously, isn't encouraging. Five wins out of nine would see them finish between 60.42 and 68.75 (depending on the remaining four results), which could suffice only if other results go their way.
India
Remaining fixtures: NZ (1 Test, away), AUS (5 Tests, home)

Even a perfect 6-0 run in their remaining games, which would take them to 66.67, isn't enough to guarantee India a place in the final. A 5-0 win over Australia at home would lift them above the 2023 champions, but they would still need either New Zealand or South Africa to drop out of the top two.

If New Zealand win the second Test in Christchurch but are then swept 4-0 by Australia, India will finish above both for certain if they win the Border-Gavaskar Trophy 5-0. A 4-0 or 4-1 result would leave them dependent on several other results, while anything less (even 3-0) could knock them out.

If India win the Christchurch Test and Australia sweep New Zealand 4-0, a 5-0 or 4-0 win for India against Australia would guarantee them a top-two finish. A 4-1 win for India would put Australia (PCT: 63.64) ahead of India (PCT: 61.11) in this scenario.
Bangladesh
Remaining fixtures: SA (1 Test, away), ENG (2 Tests, home)
England
Remaining fixtures: SA (3 Tests, away), BAN (2 Tests, away)

Both Bangladesh and England are precariously placed in the table and have only a very narrow chance of making it. Wins in all five of their remaining Tests would take England to 53.17, while Bangladesh would finish on 55.56 if they win all three.
Even then, both would have only an outside chance, needing a combination of results to go their way, and England's history of slow over rates hurts their case further.

news.title: 'Probably got away with that one': Latham after Wellington draw
news.excerpt: New Zealand, who were 70/5 on the opening day, also entered the final session of the final day at five down in the 2nd second innings
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Tom Latham conceded New Zealand had "probably got away with" one after Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips batted out the final session at the Basin Reserve to save the first Test against India. The New Zealand captain said the rearguard was a test his side had rarely faced in recent years, with Test matches now routinely finishing inside four days.

New Zealand had resumed on the final morning at 119 for 2, still a long way behind India's 720 for 9 declared. They lost Devon Conway, Rachin Ravindra and Tom Blundell before Mitchell and Phillips came together and saw off 43 overs. Shubman Gill called it off with an hour to play and the hosts at 239 for 5. Mitchell was unbeaten on 49 off 186 balls and Phillips on 26 off 126.

"It's slightly different when you're not necessarily worried about runs. It's more about time," Latham said. "But the way those guys were able to apply themselves and stick to their plans for a long period of time and ultimately get the draw... I guess that's one that we've probably got away with. They looked really clear, looked really calm, and it was a situation that we haven't necessarily been faced with for a period of time, to play in a slightly different way and adapt to what was required."

Latham was especially full of praise for Mitchell, whom he described as a player built for exactly this kind of situation. "He loves playing for this group, whatever format it may be, and I know he loves playing Test cricket. I think it's his favourite format, and he certainly showed that today," he said. "He's played some really important innings for us all around the world in different situations, whether it be attacking or defending. He's a guy for a bit of a crisis, and again he put his hand up today."

India's fast bowlers had sent down close to 50 overs each in the match. Gill admitted afterwards that the pitch had too little in it for another 10 or 15 overs to make a difference. Only 24 wickets fell across the five days, and Latham agreed the surface was not the Basin Reserve pitch New Zealand were used to. "It's probably not your traditional Basin surface that we've been presented with over the last few years," he said. "A traditional Basin wicket is where it keeps its pace and bounce, and we probably didn't see that from day two onwards. It's a little bit [of a] cliché, but it's about trying to adapt to conditions as best we can."

He also backed Gill's complaint that the ball had gone soft too early. "I think he's spot on in terms of the ball," Latham said. "Apart from day one, where the wicket probably had a little bit more in it, the ball tended to get soft. You get through those first ten overs with a new ball and things look slightly different, whereas the usual characteristic of grounds in New Zealand is that the ball stays a bit harder and probably swings for a little bit longer." On Gill's call to relax the saliva ban, though, Latham said the rules were "not necessarily up to me". He doubted there would be any change, given what the world had been through.

The draw knocked New Zealand from second to third in the World Test Championship standings, with a series against second-placed Australia to come. It also means the series will be decided at Hagley Oval from Friday. Latham argued that the result counted for more than it looked. "The introduction of the World Test Championship has put a lot of context into Test cricket," he said. "It was nice to come away with the draw here, and the importance of not just falling over and ending the game... draws become important as well."

Latham himself made a pair, but he said he wasn't concerned about his own form. "It's about trying to do my role as best I can, whatever that may look like," he said. "I certainly understand from an opener's point of view, it can be hard at times, and I try to stay reasonably calm in those moments. I've played a few Test matches now, and hopefully I'll be able to lean back on those experiences."

news.title: Unresponsive pitch, soft ball made it difficult for bowlers, says Gill
news.excerpt: The Indian captain also defended Mohammed Siraj's exclusion, stating that the tourists picked their best bowling combination for the game
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Shubman Gill admitted that India were frustrated at not being able to force a result in Wellington, but felt there was nothing more they could have done on a surface that offered very little assistance to the bowlers through the first Test. New Zealand batted out 120 overs in their second innings to secure a draw, with Gill pointing to the flattening pitch and the ball losing its hardness early as major factors that made it difficult for India to take 20 wickets.

"Yes, I do feel a little frustrated. I didn't get the result that I wanted. But this is also a part of the game. We haven't drawn that many matches in the last six or seven years," Gill said at the post-match press conference.

India had New Zealand under pressure at 70 for 5 in the first innings before Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips staged a remarkable recovery, with the hosts posting 368. The visitors responded with 720 for 9 declared, but could not make regular inroads in the second innings as the home side batted through the final day, finishing at 239 for 5.
Daryl Mitchell and Tom Blundell blunted the Indian attack with an unbroken 63-run stand, as their marathon sixth-wicket stand lasted 43 overs before the players shook hands for the draw.
Gill felt the surface had become progressively flatter, leaving the bowlers very little to work with.

"When we started playing the Test match, we thought there would be a lot more in the wicket. Days three, four and five just got flatter and flatter. There was no impact of the overs being bowled on the wicket, or even the days being played. The wicket just got slower. Having seen that, I think it wasn't a great Test wicket, especially if you want results," he said.

Gill also pointed to the condition of the ball, revealing that it had become soft within 25-30 overs, making it difficult for the bowlers to generate enough movement or carry off the surface. He also questioned why the use of saliva, which was prohibited during the COVID-19 pandemic, continued to be disallowed.

"If the wicket doesn't help and the ball also becomes soft, it becomes very difficult for the bowlers to take wickets. They don't carry the edges. If there isn't much movement in the pitch, it becomes difficult to get batters out through LBWs as well. The ball definitely plays a big role," he said.

"We saw this in England as well. In the first three or four matches, the ball became soft very quickly. After 50 overs, the ball obviously will go soft, but if it is happening after 25-30 overs, it makes the job of the bowlers very difficult.

"I don't understand one thing: it's been so long since COVID, why hasn't the ball been allowed to be shined with saliva yet? We are way past COVID times. I do believe teams should be allowed to use saliva," added Gill.
Gill defends Siraj's exclusion

The Indian captain also defended the decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI, describing it as a difficult call. Gill, however, maintained that the team had picked the best bowling attack for the conditions and backed the need to make selection decisions based on form.

"Siraj is a great player and a great bowler who has done very well for India. Before all of that, he's a really good friend of mine. We made our debuts together; even before playing for India, we were really good friends. Leaving him behind was a very tough decision for me as well," Gill said.

"But sometimes you have to see which bowlers are in form and which bowlers are bowling the best. I had this conversation with him and told him before the match that he was going to miss out. I don't know if he agreed or not, but he understood the logic behind it and why we picked someone else ahead of him. He's one of those characters who always wants to come back and do well for the team."

Asked whether India would consider changes to their combination for the next game, Gill indicated that the team was unlikely to make wholesale changes, although the nature of the pitch would remain a key consideration.

"Honestly, not really. Maybe we'll see how the wicket is, but I think most of the team is going to be the same. I thought everyone did decently well. All our bowlers did well. I don't think the batting would have done anything more. Most of the team would almost be similar, but again, we'll go there and see how the wicket is. This wicket didn't play out how we thought it was going to, so we'll see once we get there."

news.title: Mitchell, Phillips stand resolute to force a stalemate in Wellington
news.excerpt: Only three wickets fell on a lifeless Basin Reserve surface on Day 5, as Mitchell and Phillips played out 43 overs together rather comfortably
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: New Zealand produced a determined batting effort to deny India a victory in the first Test in Wellington, grinding out 120 overs in their second innings to secure a draw. Despite losing two wickets in the morning session on the final day, the hosts frustrated India through the day, with Daryl Mitchell (49* off 186) and Glenn Phillips (26* off 126) adding an unbroken 63-run stand to take their side to 239 for 5.

It was a slow and windy morning in Wellington, with only 38 runs coming off the 26 overs bowled in the first session at a rate of 1.46. India, however, managed to break through twice, ending a stubborn second-wicket partnership between Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra that had yielded 72 runs in more than 200 deliveries. The pair had largely been content to see off the Indian bowlers with their defensive approach, and the occasional boundary. Nearly an hour into the session, Washington Sundar finally broke through, aided by the wind that helped generate some drift. Conway (65 off 165) got an inside edge that deflected off his pad and ballooned into Rishabh Pant's gloves. Meanwhile, Jasprit Bumrah was handed an official warning for running on the pitch.

Shubman Gill rotated his bowling options, bringing Prasidh Krishna into the attack in the second hour. The lanky pacer struck when Ravindra went for a drive but was undone by a ball that stopped a bit on him, resulting in an edge to gully where KL Rahul took a sharp catch. Ravindra departed for 37 off 129. Tom Blundell and Daryl Mitchell then dug in, negotiating the remainder of the session without further damage.

Early in the second session, India missed a run-out opportunity to give Mitchell a lucky break as Akash Deep did not gather the ball properly at mid on. Skipper Gill was livid with the effort but a couple of overs later, he managed a smile as Anshul Kamboj got Blundell to edge behind, with India using the DRS to get the decision in their favour, leaving New Zealand at 176 for 5. India took the second new ball at the start of the 83rd over, with Bumrah getting the first crack, and Akash Deep from the other end. Mitchell and Glenn Phillips managed a boundary each ahead of the drinks break.

Phillips punched Akash Deep through cover for a four to take New Zealand past 200. Prasidh replaced Bumrah and had Mitchell in trouble, but the absence of a fielder at forward short-leg, for what would have been a simple catch, denied India another chance. The umpire's call of not-out saved Phillips when Washington rapped him on the pad and India opted for the DRS. Mitchell and Phillips saw through the period before Tea, with New Zealand keeping India at bay in another slow session that yielded 49 runs in 25 overs, at a scoring rate of 1.96, for one wicket.

Washington went for runs at the start of the third session as Mitchell targeted him and started scoring freely, including a pull for the first six of the innings. Kamboj didn't create any chances from the other end either, as Mitchell and Blundell raised a half-century stand. Akash Deep came on soon enough and bowled stump to stump lines with the 'keeper up, with Washington continuing from the other end. But they weren't able to make inroads despite keeping things tight, with Gill eventually turning to Bumrah again.

Bumrah tried his best to break through, as did Prasidh who came on sometime later, but to no avail as Mitchell and Phillips remained untroubled on a Day 5 pitch that still wasn't offering anything even into the final session. They burned a review when Washington pinned Mitchell on the pad, with the ball having pitched outside leg. Even Yashasvi Jaiswal and Dhruv Jurel were given the ball but the New Zealand batters didn't budge as Mitchell and Phillips saw off 258 deliveries in the sixth wicket partnership, before the players shook hands ahead of the final hour.

Barring the five-wicket burst on Day 1, it was hard work for the bowlers throughout the Test match. New Zealand posted 368 in the first innings after being reduced to 70 for 5, with Henry Nicholls (175*) and Phillips (118) coming to the home team's rescue. India responded with 720 for 9 declared, riding on six fifty-plus scores - centuries for Rahul and Pant, 98 for Gill, 80s from Jaiswal and Devdutt Padikkal, and 78 by Jurel. New Zealand's second-innings effort was led by Conway (65) and Mitchell, ensuring that the contest ended in a stalemate.

Brief scores: New Zealand 368 (Henry Nicholls 175*, Glenn Phillips 118; Jasprit Bumrah 4-92, Akash Deep 3-53) & 239/5 (Devon Conway 65, Daryl Mitchell 49*; Prasidh Krishna 2-23) drew with India 720/9 decl. (KL Rahul 136, Rishabh Pant 128, Shubman Gill 98, Yashasvi Jaiswal 85, Devdutt Padikkal 80, Dhruv Jurel 78; Glenn Phillips 3-154).

news.title: Allen, Tariq power Knight Riders to winning start
news.excerpt: Earlier in the day, Gulf Giants held their nerve to prevail over Sharjah Warriorz by 7 runs
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Sharjah Warriorz vs Gulf Giants

Gulf Giants made a thrilling start to their ILT20 campaign, securing a 7-run win over Sharjah Warriorz at the Sharjah Cricket Stadium on Sunday (November 7). Asked to bat first in an afternoon fixture, the Giants rode on Ibrahim Zadran’s sparkling 84 and David Miller’s 47 to post 168/8. A disciplined bowling effort, led by David Wiese (2/16) and Azmatullah Omarzai, then restricted the Warriorz to 161/7.

The Giants lost two wickets in the Powerplay, although Zadran was off the blocks quickly. Azmatullah Omarzai counter-attacked with a breezy 17 but after he and captain Heinrich Klaasen fell in quick succession, it was an 88-run stand between Zadran and Miller that revived the innings. Zadran struck six sixes in his 53-ball knock before falling to Junaid Siddique, who was the pick of the Warriorz bowlers. The innings then ended with two wickets off the last two balls, including a run out, as only 21 runs came off the last three overs.

Tim Seifert and Paul Walter then blazed away for the Warriorz, with 24 runs coming off the fourth over bowled by Alzarri Joseph. Walter’s 24-ball 40 set the foundation up for the chase, but regular wickets stunted their progress despite James Vince anchoring them with a 26-ball 31. They eventually needed 41 off the last four overs and a masterful death bowling display by Omarzai and Wiese left the Warriorz requiring 20 off the last. Joseph speared a wide down the leg-side to the fence and conceded a boundary, but he held his nerve as Mohammad Nabi fell off the last ball for 39.

Brief Scores: Gulf Giants 168/8 in 20 overs (Ibrahim Zadran 84, David Miller 47; Junaid Siddique 2-30, Adam Milne 2-33) beat Sharjah Warriorz 161/7 in 20 overs (Paul Walter 40, Mohammad Nabi 39; David Wiese 2-16, Haider Razzaq 1-24) by 7 runs.
Abu Dhabi Knight Riders vs Dubai Capitals

Abu Dhabi Knight Riders kickstarted their campaign with a resounding 55-run victory over Dubai Capitals at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium. Finn Allen's 74 and Andre Fletcher's 55 set the tone as the duo forged 119-run opening stand as the Knight Riders scored 167/6, before Usman Tariq's 4 for 27 and Muhammad Rohid Khan's 3 for 11 bowled the Capitals out for 112 in 17.5 overs.

The Knight Riders picked up pace after mustering just 13 off the first 3.5 overs as Allen broke free with a six. There was no stopping his mojo as he accelerated to a 29-ball fifty, taking Marcus Stoinis down in a 23-run 11th over. He was soon bowled by Noor Ahmad, forcing a slowdown as the Capitals’ bowlers bounced back despite Fletcher getting to his fifty. The West Indian opener took 49 balls for his 55 and was also bowled by Noor and a spurt of late wickets meant that the Knight Riders never got the final kick they were after.

As it turned out though, their total of 167 proved more than sufficient. Rohid struck twice in the second over to remove Faf du Plessis and Masood Gurbaz, before Jason Holder dismissed Max Holden soon after. At 6 for 3, the Capitals were in dire straits and it got worse when Sam Billings and Hassan Khan fell in successive overs. Usman Tariq then ran through the lower order and despite Stoinis’ 32-ball 47, the result was a formality as Rohid castled Noor to wrap things up.

Brief Scores: Abu Dhabi Knight Riders 167/6 in 20 overs (Finn Allen 74, Andre Fletcher 55; Karim Janat 2-8, Dushmantha Chameera 2-25) beat Dubai Capitals 112 in 17.5 overs (Marcus Stoinis 47; Usman Tariq 4-27, Muhammad Rohid Khan 3-11, Sunil Narine 1-12) by 55 runs.

news.title: MCC says India-Pakistan handshake issue is beyond its control
news.excerpt: While expressing a desire to see players shake hands, MCC Laws Manager Fraser Stewart says geopolitical issues and directives from above are beyond the custodians of cricket's laws
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: For perhaps the umpteenth time in cricket, India and Pakistan players did not shake hands and exchange warmth, either before or after the game. There were cold vibes between the players, whose body language remained stoic, as the India A Rising Stars side returned to the dressing room after losing to Pakistani  counterparts in Doha on Sunday (November 22). It has been happening since last year's Asia Cup in Dubai. Almost every Indian cricket team, though not necessarily teams in other sports, has avoided shaking hands with Pakistani players. So it was no surprise when Tilak Varma's team also maintained the cold shoulder towards their Pakistani counterparts. But is it wrong? Is it illegal? Against the spirit of the game? Or is it being stretched too far? The Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC), the custodians of the game's laws, say that while it would like to see players shaking hands, it cannot insist on the practice when circumstances are different, particularly when instructions come from the top.  “If there are edicts coming from above about handshakes, that's not something that MCC can control. We would like to see it, but we realise there are bigger issues at play, and that's something beyond our control,” Fraser Stewart, Laws Manager and Head of Cricket of the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC). Stewart is in UAE for the ongoing Season 5 of ILT20. “I think there are certain instances that transcend cricket and come from a level that is above my station to comment on, such as geopolitical situations. What we can control is what happens on the field. The players respect each other, they respect the umpires and the authority of the umpires, and they respect the game. That's what we can control.” The MCC official also weighed in on the Sandpapergate that is dominating the discourse in the cricket world currently. “I think my line on that would be that as far as the laws of cricket are concerned, what happened using sandpaper on the ball is a clear breach of the law. And I don't think anyone is doubting that that was the case, that what goes on and who knows what, and wait eight years and make further allegations. That's not really something for MCC to comment on. “Obviously, we want cricket to be referred to on the back pages of the papers rather than the front pages. But it's not really my place to say who's right and wrong. But from a law's perspective, using sandpaper on the ball is clearly illegal and it's right that there were punishments for that,” Stewart remarked.  On claims and counterclaims in Australian cricket over knowledge of sandpaper use in the Port Elizabeth and Cape Town Tests in 2018, the MCC official said, “There are fairly entrenched views on either side. I don't know what the truth is. That would be for Cricket Australia and others to investigate. “We have Australia coming to England for a hotly anticipated Ashes series next summer. Hopefully, by then people will let the cricket do the talking.”

news.title: Simmons urges players to step up in absence of seniors in South Africa Test
news.excerpt: Bangladesh will be without Mushfiqur Rahim and Hasan Mahmud
news.author: Atif Azam
body: Bangladesh coach Phil Simmons has called on the rest of the squad to step up as the visitors prepare to take on South Africa in the second Test without Mushfiqur Rahim and Hasan Mahmud, both ruled out with injuries.

Hasan has been ruled out of the series-concluding Test at Centurion with tennis elbow, while Mushfiqur is unavailable after sustaining a groin injury ahead of the decider. Bangladesh trail 0-1 after losing the opening Test by nine wickets.

"We saw in the last two Test matches when the other senior player Mominul wasn't there, Hridoy could step up," Simmons said. "So that's how we are trying to work it, that whoever comes in for him will step up and do what we ask them to do. That's why they're here.
"Hasan is gone, but we have four other fast bowlers here, so somebody has to take his workload."
Simmons also said Bangladesh had backed Mominul Haque through his recent lean patch, with a decision on his place in the XI to be taken after Sunday's training session.
Mominul, who scored 13 Test centuries in his career, made scores of 0 and 1 in the opening Test. He has not registered a half-century in his last 10 innings and averages around 10 in South Africa.

"Sometimes we say that senior players, and players who've scored 13 Test hundreds, must know what they're doing in some way. So yes, he's struggled for a while, but again he's working hard, he's trying to get back that form. Sometimes you have to back players for a little bit longer," Simmons said.
"In this case, we have backed him. As I said, today we will sit down and decide what is to happen from tomorrow."
The Bangladesh coach also indicated that the team was yet to decide whether to field four fast bowlers, saying the composition would depend on the conditions and the balance they wanted to strike.

"We're going to decide today when we see the wicket. Yes, people come here and play four pacers, but that's the makeup of their team and that was the balance that helped them. So we have to look at the balance that helps the Bangladesh team in this Test match," he said.

Simmons identified the bowlers' lines and lengths as one of the key areas Bangladesh needed to improve after the opening Test. He felt they had not made the South African batters play often enough, particularly around the off stump and fourth-stump channels.

"I think the main lesson that we would have spoken about a lot is the lines that we bowl to them. We don't feel that we made them play enough, and that's one of the things that we have to improve on," he said.
"I think scoring 400 in the first innings is a great thing, coming from 120 for 5, so that's a good thing. We need to improve on how often we make the batsmen play on the off stump and fourth stump."

news.title: Batter Pant, Pant banter: India's two-sided show stealer in Wellington
news.excerpt: When on song with the bat, Rishabh Pant doesn't spare anyone. Neither does he with his words, not even his own teammates
news.author: Bharat Sundaresan
body: “Main leg spin daal sakta hoon….ganda sa action chahiye toh Jaiswal daal sakta hai…”

It was one of the many standout lines that emanated from behind the stumps, courtesy Rishabh Pant as New Zealand battled away late on Sunday. It was Pant imploring his captain Shubman Gill to throw him the ball for some “leg spin” as the visitors looked to find a way to break the partnership between Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra. His other suggestion was Yashasvi Jaiswal with the “ugly action”.

It was during a period of play when the forever-ebullient wicket-keeper had found his voice. Not like he generally goes too long without finding it. But this was Pant at his absolutely menacing best with his keeping gloves on. And nobody was going to be spared. Starting with his bowlers but including the other fielders and the opposition batters. Even if most of his banter was in Hindi. Even if most of it made little sense at times to anyone else but Pant.

“He is ready to mingle..” he yelled out at one point towards the end of the over as Conway shouldered his arms to a delivery outside off-stump. The New Zealand opener didn’t seem to fathom what Pant was on about, neither did any of his Indian teammates around the bat.

It wasn’t all just random though. There were things that the 29-year-old was noticing about the surface and how the Kiwi batters were dealing with it too. Not surprisingly, since his eyes do catch everything.

“Yeh length mein dikkat ho raha hai,” he exclaimed at one point while Henry Nicholls was still out batting, having started from where he left off in the first innings. It was after an Anshul Kamboj delivery that pitched around 9 meters from the pitch, just short of a good length, and cramped the left-hander, who jammed his bat down uncomfortably at the ball. “He’s having some issues with this length,” is what Pant was trying to tell his captain.

As it turned out, this happened to be a rather prudent observation. For, Gill immediately pivoted to a new plan, one where he crammed the leg-side up with fielders, leaving only a ring field of three on the off-side. In came the leg gully, a square leg, a deepish short leg, a short mid-wicket and a couple of others to this side, as Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna, who’d just entered the attack, began peppering that length repeatedly from around the wicket.

It took only a handful of overs before Krishna had Nicholls prodding at one, getting an inside-edge and having him caught brilliantly by Dhruv Jurel who dived forward and clung on to a spectacular short-leg catch. The plan had worked. The trap had been successful, and India had got rid of probably their biggest thorn en route to a famous win at the Basin Reserve.

The Nicholls’ wicket is what triggered Pant’s most vocal session, which lasted for the rest of the day’s play. At one point, he even screamed, “Chup nahi hona abhi..” (We can’t go quiet here) when Ravindra and Conway started to get their eye in. To their credit, the two Wellingtonian left-handers survived the remaining hour or so and will resume on Day 5 as the home team look to salvage a famous draw on a pitch which still continues to remain largely in their favour. Despite all of Pant’s efforts to keep his teammates entertained and the Kiwi batters on their toes.

It had been the Rishabh Pant show all day long though. He’d been at his menacing best with bat in hand during the first half of the day scoring his 9th Test hundred, and probably among his most destructive yet. The stage had been set for the enigmatic wicket-keeper well before he even strode out to bat the previous evening. And he didn’t disappoint. It started off as a calculated assault but soon turned into a brutal and merciless onslaught as Pant tore into a tired Kiwi attack with some shots even wildly outrageous by his own standards. There were also the usual array of ramps and reverse ramps, even a reverse paddle, and a range of big hits while he moved and rolled around his crease.

If the Black Caps weren’t already batted into the ground by the likes of Jaiswal, Rahul, Gill and Devdutt Padikkal, Pant simply got them to tap out and submit. And like always, it was as entertaining as ever. No wonder so many of his peers talk about the Rishabh Pant way being the most envious of methods to play cricket. His innings included six sixes, taking him within 30 of Ben Stokes’ all-time record—138 in 122 Tests. Pant has 108 and this is still only his 53rd Test. His runs tally is ticking along rather rapidly too, with the Indian dynamo now 9th on the all-time list for wicket-keepers with most Test runs. But within 600 runs of jumping into the top 5. The form he’s in, it shouldn’t take too long for him you’d think.

For now, though, Pant’s focus like with the Indian team, will be on getting his bowlers ready to mingle with a pitch that has played hard to get so far in terms of providing any joy to them, and in turn creating a lot more dikkat for the Kiwi batters as they look to hang on grimly. Regardless, Rishabh will be there chatting away and holding court as always.

news.title: SMAT 2026: Jitesh, Samad star in thrilling chases
news.excerpt: Elsewhere, debutant Jamshed Alam had a spectacular start to his T20 career, snaring four wickets in four balls for Railways against Saurashtra
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Openers Atharva Taide and Danish Malewar laid the base for Vidarbha’s chase in a rain-hit 13-overs-a-side game against Gujarat. Despite a late hiccup, Vidarbha chased down 129 off the penultimate ball. Earlier, Gujarat suffered a collapse of their own, after openers Aarya Desai (41 off 23) and Urvil Patel (35 off 16) raced to a quick start. Parth Rekhade’s three-fer kept them under 130.

Himachal captain Pukhraj Mann struck 61 off 31, trumping his opposite number Manisankar Murasingh’s four-fer to carry them to 183 against Tripura. Then Rohit Kumar and Aryaman Dhaliwal took three each, first reducing them to 37/3, and eventually leaving them 32 runs short, despite a fighting fifty from No.5 Lakshay Thareja.

Keeper Kunal Singh Rathore’s unbeaten century was the highlight of Rajasthan’s 67-run win over Mizoram. Helped by cameos from the middle-order trio of Kartik Sharma, Mukul Choudhary and Mahipal Lomror, they racked up 224/5. Chinmay Sutar continued his fine batting run with a 25-ball 48, but Mizoram fell comfortably short.

Debutant Jamshed Alam had a spectacular start to his T20 career, snaring four wickets in four balls for Railways against Saurashtra. As many as five Saurashtra players fell for ducks, and Alam finished with 5 for 38. Chasing 183, a lone effort by Harvansh Pangalia (80) couldn’t stand against Alam’s dream debut, even as Krains Fuletra at No.10 smashed 36 off 23 alongside U19 hero Mohit Ulva (22 off 15) to reduce the defeat margin.

Mumbai cruised to a nine-wicket win over Chattisgarh, with Angkrish Raghuvanshi bouncing back from a duck to score 84* in a chase of 160. Hardik Tamore (41) and Musheer Khan (29) added useful support acts. Earlier, Shivam Dube was the pick of the bowlers, taking 3 for 21. Chattisgarh’s 17-year-old sensation Vikalp Tiwari struck 41 off 18 – eight fours included – but didn’t get much support from the rest of the top order.

Sanju Samson fell for 17 off 9, but fifties from keeper-opener Mohammed Azharuddin and Rohan Kunnummal, and a brisk cameo by Vishnu Vinod propelled Kerala to 204/4. MD Nidheesh then cut through Puducherry’s top order. Despite Prasad Pawar’s 67, and brisk knocks from Ankit Sharma (45) and Sagar Trivedi (34), Kerala were left 18 short.

The in-form Priyansh Arya fired again as part of a dominating performance by Delhi’s top-order, with contributions from Yash Dhull and Nitish Rana powering them to 232/6. But the headliner was Tejasvi Dahiya at No.4, smashing 95 off 36. In response, Haryana couldn’t match the scoring rate, with Suyash Sharma finishing with a three-fer, and Mayank Yadav taking two.

Veteran left-arm seamer Chama Milind took four as Uttarakhand were bowled out for 146 against Hyderabad. His new-ball partner Chinntla Readdi took three, as a top-order collapse first, and another towards the end saw them lose their last six for 22 runs. Hyderabad’s pursuit was held together by Kodimela Himateja’s 77, and despite wickets falling around him, it was enough to wrap up the chase in the 16th over.

Jitesh Sharma’s 54 off 29 outshone Abhimanyu Easwaran’s 78 off 46, starring in Baroda’s chase of 173 against Bengal. Skipper Krunal Pandya and Safvan Patel claimed identical figures of 2-33, hitting Bengal in different phases of their innings. Baroda’s reply was anchored by Shashwat Rawat’s 51 off 35, before Jitesh’s blitz took them through.

Madhya Pradesh eked out a five-run win over Maharashtra, surviving a late Arshin Kulkarni fifty that nearly took the game from them. Two run outs of the last two balls ended Maharashtra’s chase, which began with fifties from openers Prithvi Shaw and Sahil Parakh. Kumar Kartikeya’s 2 for 33 slowed them down in the middle before Kulkarni hauled them up. MP’s openers Harsh Gawali and Akshat Raghuwanshi, too, hit fifties, while Rajat Patidar struck 31 off 18, helping them to 208/9.

Karnataka were shot out for 95 against Chandigarh, with Hardik Chowdhry and Bhagmender Lather taking three each to never really allow them to let going. Karun Nair was the top-scorer with 25 off 22. In reply, captain Shivam Bhambri struck a fifty to polish off the chase in 14 overs.

Jammu & Kashmir pulled off a stunning chase against Punjab, with Abdul Samad’s 64* off 27 taking them through. No.7 Lone Muzaffar hit a six off the penultimate ball, lending support to Samad who hit seven sixes in his blitz. Opener Qamran Iqbal set the base with a fifty, before Harpreet Brar’s spell slowed them down. Punjab’s total of 195 was anchored by Vivaan Malhotra’s 85 off 59, while Ramandeep Singh brought up a fifty in the backend.
Note: All three Plate matches (Arunachal Pradesh vs Nagaland, Sikkim vs Meghalaya and Services vs Meghalaya) in Sovima, Nagaland were abandoned due to rain.

news.title: Injuries won't take the sting out of Centurion Test
news.excerpt: Notwithstanding Bangladesh’s competitive performance in Johannesburg, South Africa will be expected to wrap up the series 2-0
news.author: Telford Vice
body: Injuries have claimed South Africa’s captain and most solid batter along with Bangladesh’s highest capped player and their only threatening bowler at the Wanderers last week. But that shouldn’t take much gloss off the second Test between South Africa and Bangladesh in Centurion, which starts on Monday.

Bangladesh’s first innings of 400 in the first Test, replete with centuries by Towhid Hridoy and Litton Das, proved they can bat on the Highveld. South Africa showed how tough they could hang by taking a lead of 157 and then bowling the visitors out again for 168.

So the removal from the Centurion equation of Temba Bavuma, Mushfiqur Rahim and Hasan Mahmud, while regrettable, shouldn’t detract from the contest. Bavuma’s 68 not out and Mahmud’s 4/118, both in the first innings, were important elements of the Johannesburg match. But the major players in that contest are still in the mix.

Kagiso Rabada looms as the biggest factor of all. He was in furious form for his 5/70 and 3/48 at the Wanderers, and could be even better at a venue where he has taken 59 wickets at an average of 17.96 and a strike rate of 31.5. That makes Centurion Rabada’s most successful home venue on all three counts.
On top of that, Anrich Nortjé’s confirmed return to South Africa’s XI won’t make the Bangladeshi batters’ task any easier.

Aiden Markram will captain in Bavuma’s absence. Markram has led in four other Tests, all of them in Asia. South Africa’s only loss under him was to Pakistan in Lahore in October 2025. Two of his wins were achieved over Bangladesh in Dhaka and Chattogram in October 2024.

Notwithstanding Bangladesh’s competitive performance in Johannesburg, South Africa will be expected to win. In 30 Tests at this ground they have been victorious in 24 with three draws and three losses. And one of those defeats was the leatherjacket Test against England in January 2000, when the corrupt Hansie Cronjé took a cash bribe and a leather jacket — for his wife — from a gambler in exchange for engineering a result in a match that was destined to be drawn after three full days were lost to rain.

South Africa’s first legitimate defeat here was suffered against Australia in February 2014, when Shaun March made 148, Steven Smith 100 and David Warner 115, and Mitchell Johnson took 7/68 and 5/59. Then India won in Centurion in December 2021, when KL Rahul scored 123 and Mohammed Shami took 5/44 and 3/63.

In Hridoy and Litton, Bangladesh have batters who can hold their own in any company. But they have no bowlers of the class of Johnson and Shami. And this is more than anything a bowler’s ground. That makes runs here especially valuable, so it’s worth pointing out that of the 29 players who have scored a century here 11 have been foreigners — four of them from Asia.
But it’s the ball that wins in Centurion, and South Africa have the better bowlers.
When: November 23 to 27, 2026; 10am local/8am GMT/1.30pm IST
Where: Centurion

What to expect: A greentop presented itself the day before the match. But that might not mean much 24 hours later. In any event, this ground is every fast bowler’s friend. Thunderstorms have been predicted for each afternoon of the match, but that might also not mean much since they mostly pass quickly.
Team news:
South Africa: Temba Bavuma is out with a calf strain. He will be replaced by Tony de Zorzi. Anrich Nortjé comes in for Dane Paterson.
Confirmed XI: Aiden Markram (capt), Marques Ackerman, Tony de Zorzi, Zubayr Hamza, Matthew Breetzke, Ryan Rickelton, Wiaan Mulder, Marco Jansen, Simon Harmer, Kagiso Rabada, Anrich Nortjé.
Bangladesh: Mushfiqur Rahim and Hasan Mahmud will miss the match with groin and elbow injuries. Khaled Ahmed has been parachuted in and is expected to play. As is Shoriful Islam.
Possible XI: Tanzid Hasan, Mahfijul Islam, Mominul Haque, Najmul Hossain Shanto (capt), Litton Das, Jaker Ali, Towhid Hridoy, Mehidy Hasan, Khaled Ahmed, Shoriful Islam, Ebadot Hossain.
What they said:

“From a batting point of view in Centurion, you’re always going to be challenged up front. Then it can become a really nice place to bat. From a bowling point of view, you can take wickets in clusters.” — the lowdown on Centurion, courtesy of Aiden Markram.

“Whoever comes in for [Mushfiqur] will step up and do what we ask them to do. That’s why they’re here. Hassan is gone but we have four other fast bowlers, so somebody has to take his workload.” — Phil Simmons looks to make the best of an unfavourable situation.

news.title: Tamim on speculation around Simmons's contract: 'You'll see many things in the future'
news.excerpt: Simmons, however, clarified that the talks around his contract, which runs until the 2027 World Cup, do not bother him
news.author: Atif Azam
body: Bangladesh Cricket Board president Tamim Iqbal on Sunday hinted at deliberations around the performance of current head coach Phil Simmons, whose contract runs till the 2027 ODI World Cup.
Simmons's future as Bangladesh head coach is under scrutiny following Bangladesh's dismal performance recently, particularly in the white-ball format.
Under Simmons's guidance, Bangladesh have won 39 out of 95 international matches.
In Tests, Bangladesh have seven wins from 18 Tests, while in ODI they have managed only 11 in 32. In T20Is Bangladesh have won 32 out of 45 games.

“See, since he's in an ongoing series, I have my own opinion, and I'm sure you'll see many things in the future,” Tamim told reporters in an impromptu press conference at the Sher-e-Bangla National Stadium.
“Right now a series is going on, so I have to respect the fact that the Bangladesh team is going to play a Test match, then the ODIs, and then the T20Is. With time, I'm sure you'll know,”  he said.
Simmons, who is currently guiding the Bangladesh team in South Africa, hardly looked bothered by all the talks regarding his contract.
“There's been no communication about the contract or anything and to answer your question it doesn't bother me,” Simmons said.
Simmons joined Bangladesh in October 2024 when the board decided to part ways with former national head coach Chandika Hathurusingha.

news.title: Will Jacks out of remainder of England's white-ball tour of Australia
news.excerpt: ECB confirmed that the all-rounder will take no further part in the series after having suffered a broken hand in the 1st T20I in Melbourne
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Will Jacks has been out of the remainder of England’s white-ball tour of Australia after breaking his hand during the first T20I in Melbourne.
ECB confirmed that the all-rounder will take no further part in the series. An update on his replacement will be announced in due course.

Jacks hurt his hand while bowling in England’s three-wicket loss to Australia in the series opener on Saturday (November 21), copping a blow from Ben Dwarshuis in his follow-through while attempting a return catch.

Bowling his third over, Jacks was struck on his bowling hand, with visuals suggesting a possible split webbing. The physio came to check up on him, and the all-rounder, visibly in pain, was forced to walk off.

The injury occurred at a crucial juncture of the game: at that point, Australia needed 12 off 8. Henry Crocombe bowled the final two deliveries of his over. But Sam Curran couldn’t defend 11 off the final one, with Jack Edwards hitting a boundary off the penultimate ball.
It completed Australia’s highest successful men’s T20I chase (188) against England. The second T20I of the five-match series will be played on Tuesday (November 24) in Queensland.

news.title: McGrath, Wolvaardt star for Adelaide Strikers again
news.excerpt: Two days after adding 100 off 66 in a chase, the pair put on 88 off 52 in Adelaide Strikers' 37-run win over Brisbane Heat
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Tahlia McGrath (64 off 36, 11x4) and Laura Wolvaardt (54 off 42, 4x2, 2x6) were front-and-center of another Adelaide Strikers victory, as they set the team up with an 88-run partnership for the third wicket. It allowed the Strikers to post 179/4 in Brisbane and then down the home side Brisbane Heat by 37 runs. After the batting duo powered through in the first innings, Zimbabwe leg-spinner Anesu Mushangwe was the pick of the bowlers for the Strikers as Heat crashed and burned to 142/9 in 20 overs.

McGrath and Wolvaardt rescued their side from 43/2 in the eighth over, and played through the middle phase to lay the platform for a late flourish. Both McGrath and Wolvaardt reached their fifties in the 16th over while the Strikers managed 70 runs off the final 30 balls. After a 17-run 16th over, Wolvaardt was dismissed in the 17th. But even that over - from Lucy Hamilton - fetched 13 runs with three fours in it. Sianna Ginger bowled a tight penultimate over for just six runs but on either side of it, Strikers took plenty to finish with 179.

Heat lost Grace Harris in the third over but had Charli Knott and Georgia Redmayne push ahead in chase. Their 38-run stand turned out to be the best of the innings as a breakthrough triggered a downward spiral for the Heat. Mushangwe kickstarted it by dismissing Knott in the eighth over and then bowled a double-wicket over in the 12th by accounting for Prendergast and Redmayne.

Heat went from 86/2 to 112/6 by the 16th over, with curtains all but down on their attempts to secure a win. Yastika Bhatia scored a fighting 35* but didn't have support as Mushangwe bagged four wickets and the pair of Amanda-Jade Wellington and Megan Schutt picked two apiece.

Brief Scores: Adelaide Strikers 179/4 in 20 overs (Tahlia McGrath 64, Laura Wolvaardt 54; Lily Basingthwaighte 2-32) beat Brisbane Heat 142/9 in 20 overs (Yastika Bhatia 35*; Anesu Mushangwe 4-23, Amanda-Jade Wellington 2-17) by 37 runs

news.title: Conway keeps New Zealand afloat after Pant's ton powers India to record 720
news.excerpt: The visitors declared on 720/9, their third-highest Test total, before claiming two wickets in the final session.
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Rishabh Pant's century and Dhruv Jurel's 78 extended India's prolific batting show in Wellington before the visitors declared at 720 for 9 - their third-highest total in Test cricket - to take a lead of 352 on Day 4 of the first Test. India also made early inroads in New Zealand's second innings, but a patient half-century from Devon Conway helped the hosts stem the damage as they ended the day at 119 for 2, still trailing by 233.

At the start of the day, nightwatchman Anshul Kamboj came out firing on all cylinders, striking two fours each off Kyle Jamieson and Nathan Smith in the first three overs to take India past 500. Pant joined the charge with a four and a six off Jamieson as the fifth-wicket pair brought up a half-century stand. It was the first time India had recorded fifty-plus partnerships for each of their first five wickets in an overseas Test. Kamboj also launched Glenn Phillips over deep midwicket for six as India made brisk progress on the fourth morning. He contributed 38 to a 68-run stand with Pant before falling to Phillips inside the first hour of play.

The New Zealand bowlers continued to toil on a flat wicket as Jurel got going with a couple of fours, while Pant raced towards the three-figure mark with strokes all around the park. A boundary off Jacob Duffy took him into the 90s before he struck a four and a six off Phillips to bring up a 135-ball century, becoming the sixth Indian to score hundreds in all SENA countries. Jurel added another boundary off Duffy before Pant struck two more sixes off Phillips as India powered past 600 for the first time against New Zealand, and extended their lead beyond 250.

Pant's fine innings, however, came to an end in the final over before Lunch when he holed out to deep midwicket off Rachin Ravindra. His dismissal ended a 75-run partnership with Jurel, making it only the fifth instance in Test cricket of a team recording fifty-plus partnerships for each of its first six wickets in an innings. India went into the break having added 143 runs in 27.5 overs at a scoring rate of 5.14, taking their lead to 261.

A steady partnership between Jurel and Washington Sundar prolonged New Zealand's misery. It was Jurel's turn to get the next fifty-plus score in the innings, which he got with a boundary off Daryl Mitchell, and another four off the same bowler took India's lead past 300. Another half-century partnership was raised - the first time in the history of Test cricket that a team had 50-plus stands in an innings for each of the first seven wickets - before Washington was bowled by Ravindra for 24. Akash Deep then hit two sixes in an over of Phillips before the offspinner bagged his wicket.

The onslaught continued and India crossed 700, with Jurel striking a four and a six off Phillips to take the lead past 350. Phillips, however, ended Jurel's stay by having him stumped, bagging his third wicket to leave India nine down. India declared soon after the dismissal, having posted the highest total in Tests against New Zealand, and also the highest in New Zealand. Meanwhile, Duffy finished with figures of 1 for 201, becoming only the third bowler to concede 200 or more in an innings.

With a mountain to climb in the third innings, New Zealand found themselves in early trouble as Tom Latham bagged a pair, edging Jasprit Bumrah behind in the opening over. Henry Nicholls got a few boundaries and was saved by the umpire's call of not-out for lbw when he decided to shoulder arms to a Bumrah delivery and India went for the DRS. Conway, who struck a couple of fours, remained unbeaten along with Nicholls as they negotiated the 11-over passage before Tea without further damage.

There was still no assistance from the pitch for the bowlers as New Zealand's second wicket pair made steady progress, bringing up a half-century stand early in the final session. India tried unorthodox fields, using close-in fielders on the legside, bowling tight lines and keeping things quiet, trying to unsettle New Zealand in a battle of patience. It worked, as the in-form Nicholls got an inside edge onto his thigh pad off Prasidh Krishna, with Jurel taking a splendid catch diving forward from a slightly deep short-leg position, to leave New Zealand at 60 for 2.

Ravindra was stuck on zero for 14 deliveries before getting off the mark with a boundary to fine leg. He settled into a good partnership with Conway as the left-handed pair kept the Indian bowlers at bay. Conway brought up his fifty with a pull for a four off Prasidh, taking New Zealand past 100. Prasidh bowled an impressive spell, keeping the two batters on their toes, but wasn't able to break through as Conway and Ravindra saw through the remainder of the day's play, having added 59 runs.

Brief scores: New Zealand 368 & 119/2 (Devon Conway 59*, Henry Nicholls 31; Prasidh Krishna 1-20) trail India 720/9 decl. (KL Rahul 136, Rishabh Pant 128, Shubman Gill 98, Yashasvi Jaiswal 85, Devdutt Padikkal 80, Dhruv Jurel 78; Glenn Phillips 3-154) by 233 runs.

news.title: Stats: India's highest away total comes with a historic Test first
news.excerpt: For the first time in the history of Test cricket, a team had 50-plus stands for each of the first seven wickets in an innings
news.author: Roshan Gede
body: All the stats highlights from Day 4 of the ongoing first Test between New Zealand and India in Wellington.
India breach 700 for the fifth time

720/9d recorded by India is now their third-highest total in Test cricket, and their highest in an away Test. It is also the highest innings total against New Zealand in Tests, bettering 660/5d by the West Indies at the same venue in 1995.
Furthermore, it’s the highest team total in New Zealand, surpassing 715/6d by the hosts against Bangladesh in Hamilton in 2019.
700-plus totals for India in Tests
England
Chennai, 2016
Sri Lanka
Brabourne, 2009
New Zealand
Wellington, 2026
Sri Lanka
Colombo (SSC), 2010
Australia
Sydney, 2004

5 - This was India’s 5th 700-plus total in Tests, a number exceeded only by Sri Lanka (7). England, Australia and the West Indies have got four each, while Pakistan and New Zealand have got two and one respectively.
India’s previous highest Test score against the Blackcaps was 583/7d in Ahmedabad in 1999. It was their second 500-plus total in New Zealand after 520 all-out at Hamilton in 2009.

Interestingly, India had totalled 722 in four innings combined on their last Test tour of New Zealand in 2020: 165 and 191 in the first Test in Wellington, followed by 242 and 124 in Christchurch. They almost bettered that in a single innings this time around.
India’s unique feat
1 - For the first time in the history of Test cricket, a team had 50-plus stands for each of the first seven wickets in an innings.

Overall, India’s seven 50-plus stands is the joint second-most in a Test innings, alongside as many for Australia in Sydney during the Ashes 2025/26. India hold the overall record with eight against England at The Oval in 2007.
It was also just the second instance of each of a team’s top five scoring 80 or more in a Test innings. The previous too, had come against New Zealand - by Pakistan (566/3d) at Abu Dhabi in 2014.
Pant's six-hitting surge and a perfect SENA tons set
108 sixes for Rishabh Pant in Tests now puts him second only to Ben Stokes (138) in the format. He surpassed Brendon McCullum’s 107 during his stroke-filled 128.
Most sixes in Test cricket
Ben Stokes
Rishabh Pant
Brendon McCullum
Adam Gilchrist

14 sixes by India is their joint third-most in a Test innings alongside as many against South Africa in Visakhapatnam in 2019. They had hit 18 against England in Rajkot in 2024, and 15 against Sri Lanka in Brabourne in 2009.
9 - This was Pant’s ninth Test ton, taking him past England’s Les Ames for the third-most tons as a designated wicketkeeper in Tests; only Adam Gilchrist (17) and Andy Flower (12) have more.

6 - The left-hander also became the sixth Indian with a Test hundred in each of the four SENA countries (South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia). Mohammad Azharuddin, Sachin Tendulkar, Rahul Dravid and Virat Kohli were the first four, before KL Rahul joined this select list on Saturday. Saeed Anwar, Younis Khan and Kumar Sangakkara are the other sub-continent batters in this club. Pant is the only batter in this list to have scored all those hundreds as a designated wicketkeeper.
A day to forget for Duffy and Latham
1/201 - Jacob Duffy's 1/201 is the second-most runs conceded by a New Zealand bowler in a Test innings, only behind 1/229 by Stephen Boock against Pakistan in Auckland in 1989.

He is the second bowler to concede 200-plus in an innings at more than run-a-ball in Test cricket history (1/201 in 33 overs at an ER of 6.09), after Zahid Mahmood (PAK), who returned 4/235 in 33 overs against England at Rawalpindi in 2022.

news.title: MI offer came out of the blue, says Uthappa
news.excerpt: New batting coach of the franchise says his endeavour will be to bring clarity among the star batters like Rohit, Suryakumar and Tilak
news.author: Vijay Tagore
body: For Robin Uthappa the Mumbai Indians job came out of the blue. Although he had been yearning for a role in the IPL, he was still taken by surprise.

“It came completely from left field. I didn't see it coming. The interest was there, though. I've been hoping that I would get a call at some point to work with a franchise because I felt I could add a lot of value,” the former India batter says.

Mumbai Indians recently announced Uthappa (41) as the batting coach in a setup headed by Kieron Pollard. “So, when the call came, the conversations happened. The interest was there from my side. I think there is a wealth of experience from playing in the IPL over so many years,” Uthappa, who featured in 46 ODIs and 13 T20Is, says reflecting on the job.

He was part of the MI team in the league's inaugural season. Ahead of the second season, he was traded to Royal Challengers Bengaluru in exchange for Zaheer Khan. Since then, he played for four more franchises – Kolkata Knight Riders, Rajasthan Royals, Chennai Super Kings and Pune Warriors. He won the IPL titles with KKR in 2012 and with CSK in 2021. In all he has played 205 IPL games.

Uthappa moved to Dubai three years ago and has since been undertaking individual coaching assignments rather than group sessions. Some of the cricketers he works with, he claims (without disclosing names), are current India internationals.

At MI, he will be working with established India stars and World Cup winners, like Rohit Sharma, Suryakumar Yadav and Tilak Varma, among others. The endeavour, he notes, will be to bring clarity to their thinking

“As established cricketers, having clarity is important. Nobody is bigger than Mother Cricket. I think everyone has been in the game long enough to know that nobody can beat Mother Cricket or supersede it. You can be as established as you want, but as athletes, you always want to have clarity before a tournament begin.

“There are a lot of things that established players require, and as coaches, we can serve them by making sure that we give them everything they need to feel ready to perform. They should feel happy and confident about where they are before a match begins. Sometimes, just being available is such a big blessing for established players. There are umpteen things you can do.”

He continues, “They don't think of themselves as World Cup champions or as captains who have won it five times. That kind of achievement adds a lot of value when you look at it from a team perspective. But you won't find individual cricketers thinking, 'I am a World Cup-winning captain. I don't need to hear anything.' Everyone is really humble.”

MI do not have explosive batters with strike rates of around 250, like Sunrisers Hyderabad and Rajasthan Royals do in Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Will they have to change their personnel? Uthappa believes that such qualities can be discovered in the existing players too.

“Honestly, I think the talent is already there in the existing side. There is enough and more talent to prove that these players are worth their weight in gold. They are capable of performing exceptionally well. I think it depends on the conversations you have with the existing players.

“(Besides) there is an auction coming up, so you have to see what possibilities there are, perhaps, to pick up one of them,” he remarks, stating something that was never heard of before about the five-time champions, “As Mumbai Indians, we feel like we are underdogs.”
